# Tumor markers

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Basics of hematology and oncology > Tumor markers*

[Original Article Link](/library/ol00BT)

---

## Summary

<u>Tumor</u> markers are biological substances that can be detected in the blood, urine, or body tissue of some <u>tumor</u> patients. Although some <u>tumor</u> markers may aid in the diagnosis of cancer, they are primarily used for monitoring treatment response and detecting cancer recurrence. <u>Tumor</u> markers are not reliable screening or diagnostic markers due to their low <u>sensitivity</u> (i.e., not elevated in all cancer patients) and low <u>specificity</u> (i.e., also elevated in benign, noncancerous conditions or otherwise healthy patients). The majority of <u>tumor</u> markers that are used in the clinical setting can be detected in the blood. A number of <u>tumor</u> markers can be detected on tissue <u>histopathology</u>. They are also referred to as <u>immunohistochemical markers</u> and can be detected using <u>immunohistochemical</u> techniques. <u>Gene mutations</u> and patterns of <u>gene expression</u> are also increasingly being used as <u>tumor</u> markers.




For details regarding specific <u>carcinomas</u> and the corresponding <u>tumor</u> markers, see the individual cancer articles.

---

## Overview

* Definition: substances (<u>hormones</u>, enzymes, <u>antigens</u>, <u>immunoglobulins</u>, glycoproteins) that can be detected in the blood, urine, or body tissue of some cancer patients

* Clinical use

* Detect cancer (does not confirm diagnosis!)

* Predict therapeutic responses

* Monitor the <u>effectiveness</u> of cancer treatment

* Detection of cancer recurrence and screening

* Limitations

* Not all patients with cancer have elevated <u>tumor</u> markers (low <u>sensitivity</u>)

* Not all patients with elevated <u>tumor</u> markers have cancer!  (low <u>specificity</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Tumor</u> markers are generally not used to screen for or diagnose cancer. However, once cancer has been diagnosed via <u>biopsy</u>, <u>tumor</u> markers can be used to predict therapeutic responses and monitor the <u>effectiveness</u> of cancer treatment.

| <br><br>* <u>AFP</u> is normally produced by the fetus → transient elevation of maternal <u>AFP</u> levels<br><br>* ↑ <u>AFP</u>: <u>abdominal wall defects</u>, <u>neural tube defects</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>AFP</u>: associated with <u>trisomy 21</u>, 18, and 13 (see <u>prenatal diagnostics</u> for details)<br><br><br> |  |
| β-<u>HCG</u> | <br><br>* Testicular <u>germ cell tumors</u> (<u>choriocarcinoma</u>, embryonal cell <u>carcinoma</u>, mixed <u>germ cell tumor</u>, <u>seminoma</u>)<br><br>* <u>Ovarian cancer</u>: <u>choriocarcinoma</u> (<u>gestational trophoblastic disease</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* If detectable in urine<br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u> marker (produced by the <u>syncytiotrophoblast</u> in the <u>placenta</u>)<br><br>* <u>Molar pregnancy</u> (<u>hydatidiform mole</u>)<br><br> |  |

> [!NOTE]
> “Alpha male, HE is a MAN:” the cancers associated with <u>alpha-fetoprotein</u> are Hepatocellular <u>carcinoma</u>, Endodermal sinus <u>tumor</u> (<u>yolk sac tumor</u>), Mixed <u>germ cell tumor</u>, Ataxia-<u>telangiectasia</u>, and Neural tube defects.




> [!NOTE]
> β-<u>hCG</u>: Hydatidiform mole, Choriocarcinoma, and Gestational trophoblastic disease are associated with the marker

## Gene mutations and changes in gene expression

Abnormal patterns of <u>gene</u> expressions and <u>gene mutations</u> from tissue samples are increasingly being used as <u>tumor</u> markers.




| <u>Gene</u> | Conditions |
| --- | --- |
| <u>ALK gene</u> rearrangement | <br><br>* <u>Non-small cell lung cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Anaplastic large cell lymphoma</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>EGFR gene</u> mutation | <br><br>* <u>Non-small cell lung cancer</u><br><br>* Certain <u>head and neck cancers</u><br><br><br> |
| HER2neu <u>receptor</u> | <br>* <u>Breast cancer</u><br><br> |
| <u>Estrogen</u> and <u>progesterone</u> <u>receptors</u> | <br>* <u>Breast cancer</u><br><br> |





References:[[9]](/library/gSYF_o)

## Immunohistochemical markers

* Definition: <u>Antigens</u> on the surface of cells that can be detected via tissue histopathological evaluation.

* Clinical relevance

* <u>Immunohistochemical markers</u> provide information about the origin and <u>immunohistochemical</u> characteristics of <u>tumor</u> cells (e.g., distribution of protein expression).

* The presence or absence of certain <u>immunohistochemical markers</u> can help establish the prognosis of disease.





| <br><u>Overview of immunohistochemical markers</u> [[1]](/library/U30b3f)[[10]](/library/gu0Fq3)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marker | Natural occurrence | Occurrence in tumors |
| Vimentin | <br>* <u>Intermediate filament</u> in the <u>cytoskeleton</u> of <u>mesenchymal</u> cells (e.g., <u>macrophages</u>, <u>fibroblasts</u>, <u>endothelial</u> cells)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Sarcomas</u><br><br>* <u>Sarcoma botryoides</u><br><br>* <u>Ewing sarcoma</u><br><br>* <u>Osteosarcoma</u><br><br>* <u>Chondrosarcoma</u><br><br>* <u>Soft tissue sarcomas</u> (e.g., <u>angiosarcoma</u>, <u>liposarcoma</u>)<br><br>* <u>GIST</u><br><br>* <u>Endometrial carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Renal cell carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Meningioma</u><br><br>* <u>Mesothelioma</u><br><br><br> |
| Desmin | <br>* <u>Intermediate filament</u> in the <u>cytoskeleton</u> of smooth and <u>skeletal muscle</u> cells<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Rhabdomyosarcoma</u><br><br>* <u>Leiomyosarcoma</u><br><br><br> |
| Mesothelin | <br>* Membrane-bound glycoprotein<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mesothelioma</u><br><br>* <u>Pancreatic</u>, esophageal, and <u>gastric carcinoma</u><br><br><br> |
| Cytokeratin | <br>* <u>Intermediate filament</u> in the <u>cytoskeleton</u> of <u>epithelial</u> cells<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Squamous cell carcinoma</u> (e.g. of the <u>skin</u> or <u>lung</u>)<br><br>* <u>Basal cell carcinoma</u><br><br><br> |
| Neurofilaments | <br>* <u>Neurons</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neuroendocrine tumors</u><br><br>* <u>Neuroblastoma</u><br><br>* <u>Medulloblastoma</u><br><br>* <u>Small cell lung cancer</u> (<u>SCLC</u>)<br><br>* <u>Merkel cell carcinoma</u><br><br><br> |
| Chromogranin A | <br>* Secretory granules of <u>neuroendocrine cells</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neuroendocrine neoplasms</u> (e.g., <u>pheochromocytoma</u>, <u>SCLC</u>)<br><br>* <u>Medullary thyroid cancer</u><br><br><br> |
| Synaptophysin | <br>* Secretory granules of <u>neuroendocrine cells</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neuroendocrine neoplasms</u> (e.g., <u>pheochromocytoma</u>, <u>SCLC</u>)<br><br>* <u>Medullary thyroid cancer</u><br><br><br> |
| S-100 | <br>* <u>Neural crest cells</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Schwannoma</u><br><br>* <u>Melanoma</u><br><br>* <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u><br><br><br> |
| GFAP | <br>* <u>Intermediate filament</u> in the <u>cytoskeleton</u> of <u>neuroglia</u> (e.g., <u>oligodendrocytes</u>, <u>astrocytes</u>, <u>Schwann cells</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Glioblastoma</u><br><br>* <u>Astrocytoma</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>PSA</u> | <br>* <u>Prostate</u> <u>epithelium</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Prostate cancer</u><br><br> |
| TRAP | <br>* Tartrate-resistant acid <u>phosphatase</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hairy cell leukemia</u><br><br> |
| <u>PECAM-1</u> | <br>* <u>Endothelial</u> cells<br><br> | <br>* Vascular tumors (e.g., <u>angiosarcoma</u>)<br><br> |
| CD20 | <br>* <u>B lymphocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>B cell</u> <u>lymphoma</u><br><br> |
| CD3 | <br>* <u>T lymphocytes</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>T cell</u> <u>lymphoma</u><br><br> |
| CD8 | <br>* <u>T killer cells</u> (cytotoxic <u>T lymphocytes</u>)<br><br> |  |
| CD4 | <br>* <u>T helper cells</u><br><br> |  |
| CD45 | <br>* <u>Hematopoietic</u> cells<br><br> | <br>* Malignant <u>lymphoma</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> DesMin is associated with muscle tumors like rhabdoMyosarcomas.




> [!NOTE]
> ViMEntin is associated with MEsenchymal tumors.




> [!NOTE]
> G<u>FAP</u> stains neuroGlial cells, which are affected in Glioblastomas.
